title: Tenant lease reclamation & TTL profile design
summary: Design for tenant-aware lease-based reclamation and approximate TTL profiling to reduce fragmentation and improve eviction quality across heterogeneous memory pools.
content:
Problem statement:

Current serving-runtime cache eviction is largely reactive and agnostic to tenant request patterns. We observe two recurring issues at scale:

1) Cross-tenant fragmentation: multiple small allocations from different tenants scatter across slabs/pools, increasing per-tenant working set footprint and causing compaction churn.
2) Poor eviction proxies: LRU or hotness sampling alone often ejects items that would have been accessed again shortly, or retains cold state for too long, inflating memory pressure and causing aggressive compaction which harms tail latency.

Goals:

- Improve eviction decision quality without large CPU overhead.
- Reduce long-term fragmentation across pools and slabs by coordinating reclamation with tenant ownership.
- Maintain tenant isolation guarantees (soft quotas) and ensure fairness under contention.
- Provide observable signals (per-tenant fragmentation, TTL distribution) and a path to gradual rollout.

High-level idea:

Introduce a lease-based reclamation layer and lightweight TTL profiling per-tenant. Each cache entry gains a short-lived lease token (micro-lease) that represents a recent access window and an estimated TTL bucket derived from access patterns. Eviction considers (lease_age, ttl_bucket, tenant_utilization) combined with pool-level fragmentation heuristics to prefer reclaiming blocks whose reclamation yields lower fragmentation amplification.

Key components:

1) Tenant Lease Token (micro-lease)
- On read/write of a cached key, issue/update a micro-lease: a 16-bit token encoding last-access bucket (log-time buckets: 0-5ms, 5-20ms, 20-200ms, 200ms-2s, 2s-30s, >30s) and a short epoch id (for staleness detection).
- Micro-lease is stored in metadata compactly (fits into 2 bytes per slot) to keep memory overhead low.
- On eviction candidate scoring, entries with very recent micro-leases (hot buckets) are deprioritized.

2) Approximate TTL Profiles
- Each tenant maintains an approximate distribution of inter-access intervals per key hashed into TTL buckets. Implementation: a small per-tenant counting sketch (count-min with decays) with 16 buckets for quantiles (sub-second up to hours).
- TTL-profile is updated on accesses and on explicit observed expirations (application-driven TTL hints when available).
- The runtime exposes TTL profile to eviction scoring so that objects predicted as short-lived are preferred for eviction before long-lived ones, reducing churn (i.e., evict many short-lifetime items first).

3) Pool-aware fragmentation score
- Each memory pool (slab class) maintains lightweight fragmentation metrics: free-run-length histogram, occupancy variance across slabs, and tenant-slot-entropy (how many tenants own slots within each slab).
- Compute a fragmentation penalty for reclaiming a slot from a particular slab. Higher penalty if reclaiming increases cross-tenant interleaving (i.e., would leave a slab with more mixed tenants).

4) Tenant lease reclamation policy (algorithm sketch)
- When pressure triggers eviction in pool P:
  a) Build candidate set from admission queue + sampling (size bounded, e.g., 64 items).
  b) For each candidate, compute score = base_priority - alpha * recent_lease_weight - beta * ttl_preference + gamma * tenant_quota_boost - delta * frag_penalty.
    - base_priority: existing hotness/LRU proxy (fast to compute).
    - recent_lease_weight: high for buckets in last 2 windows -> avoid evicting hot items.
    - ttl_preference: positive for buckets that indicate short expected lifetime.
    - tenant_quota_boost: a boost to favor evicting from over-quota tenants to enforce fairness.
    - frag_penalty: computed from slab-level metrics to avoid choices that increase fragmentation.
  c) Select candidate(s) with highest score for eviction.

Tradeoffs and cost model:

- Metadata overhead: ~2 bytes per slot for lease token + amortized ~0.5-1 bytes per slot for sketches (shared across tenant pools) — target <3 bytes/slot.
- CPU overhead: per-access updates are tiny bitops and counters (increment a bucket, occasionally decay). Eviction scoring is slightly heavier but bounded by candidate set size.
- Accuracy vs cost: Using coarse TTL buckets and tiny sketches sacrifices per-key precision but yields good aggregated eviction decisions with low memory/CPU cost.

Fragmentation mitigation actions:

- Prefer tenant-homogeneous slab consolidation: when a slab becomes underused and >70% of occupied slots belong to a single tenant, mark it for tenant-directed compaction (migrate live entries to a different slab to free contiguous space).
- Trigger opportunistic compaction during low load windows; schedule background compaction at per-pool rate limits to bound CPU.
- Introduce a "slab swap" operation: rather than moving many small items, allocate a clean slab and migrate a tenant's hot working set onto it in one batch to reduce transient fragmentation.

Rollout plan (staged):

1) Simulation & offline replay (2-3 weeks): run the scoring algorithm against historical access traces (hosted API + Dedicated traces) to measure hit-rate, tail latency impact, compaction frequency, and tenant fairness under contention.
2) Canary in non-critical region: enable lease tokens + TTL profiling in read-only scoring (i.e., collect scores but do not change eviction outcome) for 1 week to validate metrics.
3) Soft enable: apply scoring but restrict to a small subset of pools (e.g., low-latency non-burst pools) and enable tenant-quota enforcement in monitor-only mode.
4) Full enable with safe-fallback: enable everywhere with ability to revert to prior policy and automatic throttling if compaction > threshold or miss-rate regresses by >X%.

Telemetry and observability:

Instrument counters and time-series for:
- per-tenant ttl_bucket distribution (periodic snapshot)
- per-pool fragmentation_score and slab_entropy
- number of tenant-directed compactions and slab-swap events
- eviction causes breakdown (lease-age, ttl-pref, frag-avoid)
- CPU cost of eviction scoring and background compaction

Dashboards:
- Tenant fairness heatmap (utilization vs eviction pressure)
- Fragmentation trend per-pool (free-run-length histogram over time)
- Regression alert: increase in average compaction operations / minute or >10% tail latency increase after rollout.

Open questions / investigations:

- Ideal bucketization: tune number and cutpoints for micro-lease and TTL buckets per workload class.
- Sketch decay policy: how aggressive should counts decay to adapt to shifting workloads?
- Interplay with prefix/KV caching semantics: some workloads have prefix locality where small prefixes dominate; eviction that favors tenants could harm global throughput.
- Multi-tenant enforcement: should we proactively move items from noisy tenants off hot slabs or impose stricter limits when a tenant causes high fragmentation?

Experiment proposals (short):

A) A/B TTL buckets: run two configurations (6 buckets vs 12 buckets) and measure hit-rate and compaction frequency.
B) Frag-penalty ablation: disable frag_penalty and measure slab fragmentation and compaction rate.
C) Tenant-boost sensitivity: vary tenant_quota_boost to find tradeoff between fairness and global hit-rate.

Appendix: Implementation notes

- Storage layout: keep micro-lease byte adjacent to existing occupancy bitmaps to leverage cache locality when sampling candidates. Place per-tenant sketch in a shared metadata shard to avoid per-slot pointer overhead.
- Concurrency: lease updates are allowed to race; use relaxed atomic increments for sketch updates. Eviction must read a consistent snapshot of lease bucket and slab frag metrics — sample ordering acceptable for probabilistic correctness.
- Backwards compatibility: fall back to current LRU/hotness scoring if new metadata not present on an entry (migration window).

Conclusion:

Tenant-lease reclamation combined with lightweight TTL profiling offers a pragmatic path to reduce fragmentation and improve eviction quality with small memory and CPU overhead. The approach prioritizes low-risk rollout, strong observability, and operator controls. Next steps: run offline trace simulations (ENG-1427), prepare canary build (PR linked), and iterate on bucketization heuristics based on initial telemetry.
